changes.old: The review notes that in most imaging studies users reported extensive other drug use while controls reported little, making methamphetamine-specific effects hard to isolate (pp. 597–598).
changes.new: The review notes that in most imaging studies the methamphetamine groups reported extensive other drug use while controls reported little, making methamphetamine-specific effects hard to isolate (pp. 597–598).

changes.old: Controlled single-dose laboratory studies found no cognitive disruption and some improvement at the doses tested; chronic-use studies found statistically significant user–control differences on a minority of measures, frequently without normative comparison, education matching or control of other drug use; several primary papers draw causal or clinical conclusions their designs cannot support.
changes.new: Controlled single-dose laboratory studies found no cognitive disruption and some improvement at the doses tested; chronic-use studies found statistically significant methamphetamine–control differences on a minority of measures, frequently without normative comparison, education matching or control of other drug use; several primary papers draw causal or clinical conclusions their designs cannot support.

changes.old: The conclusion states that the widely publicized methamphetamine–cognitive impairment link is not supported by research evidence (p. 605) and that concerns about cognitive deficits compromising engagement in cognitive-behavioural treatment are not warranted (p. 605). The review's own material shows the link is not established, not that it is refuted: significant differences exist on some measures, and individual-level impairment in a minority of users is documented in one study it discusses (Kalechstein et al., 2003, p. 602). The normative re-analyses that carry much of the argument are not reproducible as reported.
changes.new: The conclusion states that the widely publicized methamphetamine–cognitive impairment link is not supported by research evidence (p. 605) and that concerns about cognitive deficits compromising engagement in cognitive-behavioural treatment are not warranted (p. 605). The review's own material shows the link is not established, not that it is refuted: significant differences exist on some measures, and individual-level impairment in a minority of people who use methamphetamine is documented in one study it discusses (Kalechstein et al., 2003, p. 602). The normative re-analyses that carry much of the argument are not reproducible as reported.

changes.old: Response review argues the preponderance of evidence supports mild cognitive decline in at least some users and rejects a categorical normal/impaired reading
changes.new: Response review argues the preponderance of evidence supports mild cognitive decline in at least some people who use methamphetamine and rejects a categorical normal/impaired reading

changes.old: The review's specific criticisms of primary studies are checkable and, for the four Volkow-group imaging papers, confirmed on reading (cognition tested in users only, no education data). Its overall conclusion remains contested; see the debate on cognition.
changes.new: The review's specific criticisms of primary studies are checkable and, for the four Volkow-group imaging papers, confirmed on reading (cognition tested in the methamphetamine group only, no education data). Its overall conclusion remains contested; see the debate on cognition.

changes.old: A pre-registered systematic review applying a normative (demographically adjusted) impairment criterion to individual-level data from all user–control studies, alongside group differences; and prospective cohorts with pre-use cognitive baselines.
changes.new: A pre-registered systematic review applying a normative (demographically adjusted) impairment criterion to individual-level data from all studies comparing people who use methamphetamine with controls, alongside group differences; and prospective cohorts with pre-use cognitive baselines.

changes.old: Under-represented: the evidence for impairment. The one meta-analysis in the reference list (Scott et al., 2007) is cited only as the source of the prevailing view (p. 587), animal evidence of deficits gets one sentence before its dosing regimens are questioned (p. 589), and each user–control difference discussed in the text is followed by reasons to doubt its clinical significance (pp. 596–604).
changes.new: Under-represented: the evidence for impairment. changes.old: In McCann et al. (1998), DAT binding in users overlapped considerably with controls, and all users reported other illicit drug use.
changes.new: In McCann et al. (1998), DAT binding in people who used methamphetamine overlapped considerably with controls, and all of them reported other illicit drug use.

changes.new: Johanson et al. (2006): DAT and VMAT2 binding 10–16% lower in 16 people abstinent from methamphetamine than 18 controls; the methamphetamine group differed on a minority of tests and stayed within the normal range for age and education; no relation between imaging and cognition.

changes.old: The reviewers compared the mean scores of users in McCann et al. (2008) and Simon et al. (2002) with published norms and found none outside the normal range; Simon et al. (2010) did not replicate the 2002 group differences.
changes.new: The reviewers compared the mean scores of the methamphetamine groups in McCann et al. (2008) and Simon et al. (2002) with published norms and found none outside the normal range; Simon et al. (2010) did not replicate the 2002 group differences.

changes.old: No pooled estimates. Vote counts: of 7 well-matched studies, 6 found users worse on some tests; of 8 statistically controlled studies, 5 did (p. 261). changes.old: Animal studies show cognitive deficits after chronic or binge dosing, partly prevented by prior dose escalation; matched cross-sectional studies mostly show users worse on a subset of tests, usually by less than 1 SD; one twin study shows mixed results; controlled longitudinal studies show no significant group-by-time recovery; brain measures change during early abstinence in small studies; dose–response is mostly absent.
changes.new: Animal studies show cognitive deficits after chronic or binge dosing, partly prevented by prior dose escalation; matched cross-sectional studies mostly show the methamphetamine groups worse on a subset of tests, usually by less than 1 SD; one twin study shows mixed results; controlled longitudinal studies show no significant group-by-time recovery; brain measures change during early abstinence in small studies; dose–response is mostly absent.

changes.old: The abstract speaks of the possibility that methamphetamine causes mild decline in some users (p. 259); the discussion states it does cause mild decline in at least some individuals (pp. 268–270). The causal step rests on combining lines of evidence that share confounds (selection, premorbid differences, practice effects) and on weighting animal evidence most heavily (p. 268) despite the dose-translation caveats the review itself raises (p. 260). Support for recovery with abstinence is called mild although both controlled longitudinal studies were null on their primary comparisons (p. 264).

Support for recovery with abstinence is called mild although both controlled longitudinal studies were null on their primary comparisons (p. 264).
